Title: Commemorative Conference of the 60th Anniversary of CEMLA
text: Presentation by Rodrigo Bolanos Zamora President of the Central Bank of Costa Rica President of the Central American Monetary Council Commemorative Conference of the 60th Anniversary of CEMLA "Cooperation between Central Banks at the Beginning of the XXI Century" Mexico City, July 19 and 20, 2012 Roundtable: Where central bank cooperation is headed I thank and congratulate the Center for Latin American Monetary Studies (CEMLA), for the much it has helped the central banks of Latin America in their 60 years of existence, but especially, as shown yesterday by the data presented by the Director General, Lic. Javier Guzman, to the central banks of smaller countries. Congratulations! I would like to concentrate my comments on some issues of future technical assistance, of special relevance to central banks of small and open economies such as Central America, based mainly on the vision from Costa Rica, but with inputs from our participation in the Central American Monetary Council (CMCA). The Council, together with CEMLA and other organizations such as the Latin American Reserve Fund (FLAR), International Monetary Fund (IMF), Regional Technical Assistance Center for Central America, Panama and the Dominican Republic (CAPTAC-DR), World Bank (WB), Inter-American Development Bank (IDB) and central banks of Mexico, Colombia, Chile, Peru, Spain, the United States of America, Germany, have taught us much of what we have managed to learn. In fact, the Central Bank of Costa Rica was born in 1950, as one of several banks created with the significant contributions of Dr. Herman Max, prestigious official of the Central Bank of Chile. Looking closely at the central banks members of the Central American Monetary Council, we will find some features that help fine-tune the type of technical assistance and cooperation we might need going forward. Like most, or all, central banks around the world, ours face the challenges and opportunities of globalization, the challenges of achieving and maintaining low inflation and more robust and stable financial systems, as well as preserving or, where necessary, increasing their independence, with the best degree of coordination of their policies with fiscal policy, commercial and financial supervision and regulation. In addition to these common internal considerations, we also share with other central banks the need to seek greater coordination with other banks, especially countries with which our economies have extensive trade and capital flow interrelations. Also, we have to coordinate and dialogue our policies with important international organizations, and participate in various forums, which help us better understand what they are doing or may be happening in the economies and central banks of countries of greater influence. Within this context, our central banks act with characteristics or restrictions somewhat different from those of larger or more developed countries, which condition where it may be most valuable to seek and obtain assistance and cooperation from other central banks, directly or through bodies such as CEMLA. As already mentioned yesterday, economic research is fundamental for better design, formulation and implementation of economic policies. The lack of economies of scale or the lack of resources of the central banks of small and low- or middle-income countries means that we are more dependent on external support. Therefore, it is very valuable, for our countries, the research carried out by international organizations, especially, but not exclusively, the IMF, an organization that can focus and carry out studies for our region and, sometimes, for individual countries, beyond the policy documents and evaluation of our economies. The forums provided by CEMLA so that our researchers can polish their work and submit them to comments and criticism, are very important, and we are greatly encouraged that these areas are strengthened in the Strategic Plan that the institution has in execution. However, I would like to emphasize here that this is one of the areas in which human resources external to the region can be highly productive. We would very much like that, in the allocation of the very valuable additional human resources that CEMLA is devoting to resuming research strongly, this particular demand or need of our CMCA member central banks can be considered, either in joint work with the Council or with one or more of the research departments of our central banks. Considering these and other characteristics of our economies not only helps us define some of the particular topics where research can be most valuable, but also helps define where cooperation with CEMLA and other central banks and agencies will be of great use to us. Another characteristic that stands out is the lack of development of several markets that are key to the conduct of economic policy in general, and monetary and financial policy in particular. Some countries are more advanced than others, but evidence suggests that in general everyone in Central America and the Dominican Republic has a long way to go in these markets. The countries of the subregion also have central banks that have once again given high priority, not exclusive, but the highest, to low inflation. For those who have a domestic currency, and even for El Salvador that was dollarized, it is crucial to have better markets in several services to keep inflation low. Banking services markets are the most developed in relative terms, but markets for liquidity, government debt, foreign exchange, securities and capital are only in their early stages of development. For example, for those of us who are moving towards inflation-targeting schemes or those who are already there, better and more efficient liquidity, exchange and public debt markets are fundamental. In addition, not only must they be improved at the level of each country, but the existence of groups Financial institutions with activities in several countries of the subregion mean that the development of these markets requires significant coordination of plans and policies between central banks and supervisors. The CMCA has played and will continue to play a fundamental role in these efforts, but here we require additional cooperation to that already provided by the central banks of more developed markets and bodies that have studied and advised other regions in these tasks. There are two other important areas for cooperation with CMCA member central banks. The first is the forums for the exchange of experiences and analysis on the global and regional economic situation provided by CEMLA, IMF, IDB, and WB, and more recently the Bank for International Settlements (BIS). In the latter case it is recent because the central banks of the CMCA have finally approached the BIS, which has always invited them. These forums are very valuable and the intention to maintain them is gratifying. The second issue has to do with the possibilities of crisis shielding. Obviously, there is the accumulation of reserves and access to the IMF. But as discussed at this conference, Latin America has not made as much progress in regional schemes as it has in other countries, particularly Asia. Costa Rica is a proud member of the Latin American Reserve Fund (FLAR), along with the central banks of six other South American countries. Unlike the Andean Development Corporation (CAF), which, as its name implies, was born as part of the Andean integration institutions, back in the 1970s, FLAR, CAF's twin brother, changed its name from the Andean Fund to the Latin American Fund, but has not yet managed to become as Latin American in membership as CAF. FLAR is a small but valuable institution, with an excellent team of professionals, very efficient and which is not only available to support its members with financing against balance of payments liquidity problems or debt restructuring, but also provides valuable cooperation for the management of international reserves, as well as forums to discuss and analyze the experience of member central banks and other relevant issues. It would be very useful if CEMLA and other forums could discuss more systematically the advisability of expanding the role of this organization in shielding against external crises, especially for smaller countries, always as a complement to other forms of protection. FLAR himself has just had a very good discussion about his role in one of his conferences in Cartagena. Perhaps, one day, the personal dream will be fulfilled that all the smaller countries in Latin America will be beneficiary members of FLAR and the larger ones will follow the example of Colombia, Peru and Venezuela (the largest FLAR members), to support the smaller ones through this organization and also can benefit from its various services and participate more actively in its discussion forums. There are many other areas of important collaboration and technical assistance going forward. In particular, in matters of macroprudential supervision and regulation, the institutional arrangements between central banks and supervisors towards the internal and external of each country, the consequences of the regulatory changes in Basel 2.5 and 3 and those applied in the economies of greater global influence such as the United States of America and Europe, among others. These issues have not only already been addressed in this conference, but they are not particular to the countries of Central America and the Dominican Republic and, in addition, they are issues in which there are already adequate forums and cooperation and where several countries of the subregion already participate. For this reason, there is no need to refer to them on this occasion. Again, many thanks to CEMLA, its Governing Board, Director General and staff, and those who preceded them in those functions, for their very valuable contribution to our tasks and for having another 60, or many more, years of success and valuable contributions to Latin America and beyond. Thanks a lot!

Javier Guzmn, a los bancos centrales de pases ms pequeos. Felicidades! Quisiera concentrar mis comentarios en algunos temas de asistencia tcnica futura, de especial relevancia para bancos centrales de economas pequeas y abiertas como las centroamericanas, basados principalmente en la visin desde Costa Rica, pero con insumos de nuestra participacin en el Consejo Monetario Centroamericano (CMCA). El Consejo, junto con CEMLA y otros organismos como el Fondo Latinoamericano de Reserva (FLAR), Fondo Monetario Internacional (FMI), Centro Regional de Asistencia Tcnica de Centroamrica, Panam y la Repblica Dominicana (CAPTAC-DR), Banco Mundial (BM), Banco Interamericano de Desarrollo (BID) y bancos centrales de Mxico, Colombia, Chile, Per, Espaa, Estados Unidos de Amrica, Alemania, nos han enseado mucho de lo que hemos logrado aprender. De hecho, el Banco Central de Costa Rica nace en 1950, como uno de los varios bancos creados con los aportes significativos del Dr. Herman Max, prestigioso funcionario del Banco Central de Chile. Visualizando de cerca a los bancos centrales miembros del Consejo Monetario Centroamericano, nos encontraremos con algunas caractersticas que ayudan a afinar el tipo de asistencia tcnica y de cooperacin que podramos necesitar hacia adelante. Como casi todos, o todos, los bancos centrales alrededor del mundo, los nuestros enfrentan los desafos y oportunidades de la globalizacin, los retos de alcanzar y mantener una inflacin baja y sistemas financieros ms robustos y estables, as como preservar o, cuando sea necesario, aumentar, su independencia, con el mejor grado de coordinacin de sus polticas con la fiscal, comercial y la de supervisin y regulacin financiera. Adems, de estas comunes consideraciones internas, tambin compartimos con otros bancos centrales la necesidad de buscar una mayor coordinacin con otros bancos, especialmente de pases con lo que nuestras economas tienen amplias interrelaciones comerciales y de flujos de capitales. Tambin, tenemos que coordinar y dialogar nuestras polticas con importantes organismos internacionales, y participar en diversos foros, que nos ayudan a entender mejor lo que estn haciendo o puede estar ocurriendo en las economas y bancos centrales de pases de mayor influencia. Dentro de ese contexto, nuestros bancos centrales actan con caractersticas o restricciones algo diferentes a los de pases de mayor tamao o desarrollo, que condicionan dnde puede ser ms valioso buscar y obtener asistencia y cooperacin de otros bancos centrales, directamente o a travs de organismos como el CEMLA. Como ya se mencion ayer, la investigacin econmica es fundamental para un mejor diseo, formulacin y ejecucin de las polticas econmicas. Las carencias de economas de escala o la falta de recursos de los bancos centrales de pases pequeos y de ingresos bajos o medios, significa que nosotros dependemos ms del apoyo externo. Por eso, es muy valiosa, para nuestros pases, la investigacin que realizan organismos internacionales, especialmente, pero no exclusivamente, el FMI, organismo que puede focalizar y hacer estudios para nuestra regin y, en ocasiones, para pases individuales, ms all de los documentos de polticas y evaluacin de nuestras economas. Los foros que nos brinda el CEMLA para que nuestros investigadores puedan pulir sus trabajos y someterlos a los comentarios y crticas, son muy importantes, y nos alienta enormemente que esas reas se fortalecen en el Plan Estratgico que la institucin tiene en ejecucin. Sin embargo, quisiera aqu enfatizar que esta es una de las reas en las que recursos humanos externos a la regin pueden sernos de alta productividad. Nos gustara mucho que, en la asignacin de los muy valiosos recursos humanos adicionales que el CEMLA est dedicando a retomar con fuerza la investigacin, se pueda considerar esta demanda o necesidad particular de nuestros bancos centrales miembros del CMCA, ya sea en trabajos conjuntos con el Consejo o con uno o varios de los departamentos de investigacin de nuestros bancos centrales. Considerar estas y otras caractersticas de nuestras economas, no solo nos ayudan a definir algunos de los temas particulares en los que la investigacin puede ser ms valiosa, sino tambin ayudan a definir dnde la cooperacin con el CEMLA y otros bancos centrales y organismos, nos ser de suma utilidad. Otra caracterstica que destaca es la falta de desarrollo de varios mercados que son claves para la conduccin de la poltica econmica en general, y la monetaria y financiera en particular. Algunos pases estn ms avanzados que otros, pero la evidencia sugiere que en general a todos en Centroamrica y Repblica Dominicana les hace falta mucho por hacer en estos mercados. Los pases de la subregin tienen tambin bancos centrales que le han vuelto a dar alta prioridad, no exclusiva, pero s de la ms alta, a una inflacin baja. Para los que tienen una moneda domstica, y an para El Salvador que se dolariz, es crucial contar con mejores mercados en varios servicios para mantener una inflacin baja. Los mercados de servicios bancarios son los ms desarrollados en trminos relativos, pero los mercados de liquidez, deuda estatal, divisas, valores y capitales, estn apenas en sus primeras etapas de desarrollo. Por ejemplo, para los que estamos avanzando hacia esquemas de metas de inflacin o los que ya estn ah, mejores y ms eficientes mercados de liquidez, cambiarios y deuda pblica son fundamentales. Adems, no solo hay que mejorarlos a nivel de cada pas, sino que la existencia de grupos financieros con actividades en varios pases de la subregin, significa que para el desarrollo de estos mercados se requiere de una importante coordinacin de los planes y polticas entre los bancos centrales y supervisores. El CMCA ha jugado y seguir jugando un papel fundamental en estos esfuerzos, pero aqu requerimos cooperacin adicional a la que ya se ha brindado por parte de los bancos centrales de mercados ms desarrollados y organismos que han estudiado y asesorado a otras regiones en estas tareas. Hay otras dos reas importantes para la cooperacin con los bancos centrales miembros del CMCA. La primera son los foros de intercambio de experiencias y anlisis sobre la situacin econmica mundial y regional que brindan el CEMLA, FMI, BID, y BM, y ms recientemente el Banco Internacional de Pagos (BIS). En este ltimo caso es reciente porque los bancos centrales del CMCA finalmente, se han acercado al BIS, que siempre los ha invitado. Estos foros son muy valiosos y es grato la intencin de mantenerlos. El segundo tema tiene que ver con las posibilidades de blindaje ante crisis. Obviamente, est la acumulacin de reservas y el acceso al FMI. Pero como se ha discutido en esta conferencia, en Amrica Latina no se han hecho tantos avances en esquemas regionales como s ha ocurrido en otros pases, particularmente Asia. Costa Rica es un orgulloso miembro del Fondo Latinoamericano de Reservas (FLAR), junto con los bancos centrales de otros seis pases de Sudamrica. A diferencia de la Corporacin Andina de Fomento (CAF), que, como su nombre lo insina, naci como parte de las instituciones de integracin andina, all en los aos 1970s, el FLAR, hermano gemelo de la CAF, se cambi el nombre de Fondo Andino a Fondo Latinoamericano, pero no ha logrado todava hacerse tan latinoamericano en membresa como la CAF. El FLAR es una pequea pero valiosa institucin, con un excelente equipo de profesionales, muy eficiente y que no solo est disponible para apoyar a sus miembros con financiamiento frente a problemas de liquidez de balanza de pagos o restructuracin de deuda, sino que tambin brinda valiosa cooperacin para la gestin de reservas internacionales, as como foros para discutir y analizar la experiencia de los bancos centrales miembros y otros temas relevantes. Sera muy til que en el CEMLA y en otros foros, se pueda discutir ms sistemticamente la conveniencia de ampliar el rol de esta organizacin en el blindaje ante crisis externas, especialmente para los pases ms pequeos, siempre como complemento de otras formas de proteccin. El propio FLAR acaba de tener una muy buena discusin sobre su rol en una de sus conferencias en Cartagena. Tal vez, algn da, se cumpla el sueo personal de que todos los pases de tamao ms pequeo de Amrica Latina sean miembros beneficiaros del FLAR y los ms grandes sigan el ejemplo de Colombia, Per y Venezuela (-los miembros del FLAR- de mayor tamao), de apoyar a los ms pequeos por medio de esta organizacin y tambin puedan beneficiarse de sus diversos servicios y que participen ms activamente en sus foros de discusin. Hay muchas otras reas de importante colaboracin y asistencia tcnica de cara al futuro. En particular, en temas de supervisin y regulacin macroprudencial, los arreglos institucionales entre bancos centrales y supervisores hacia lo interno y a lo externo de cada pas, las consecuencias de los cambios regulatorios en Basilea 2.5 y 3 y las aplicadas en las economas de mayor influencia mundial como Estados Unidos de Amrica y Europa, entre otros. Estos temas no solo ya se han tratado en esta conferencia, sino que no son particulares a los pases de Centroamrica y Repblica Dominicana y, adems, son temas en los que ya hay foros y cooperacin adecuados y donde ya varios pases de la subregin participan. Por tal razn, no hace falta referirse a ellos en esta oportunidad. De nuevo muchas gracias al CEMLA, a su Junta de Gobierno, Director General y personal, y a los que les precedieron en esas funciones, por su muy valiosa contribucin a nuestras tareas y que tengan otros 60, o muchos ms, aos de xitos y valiosos aportes a Latinoamrica y ms all. Muchas Gracias!

Title: The Central Bank, inflation and economic growth
text: The Central Bank, inflation and economic growth By: Olivier Castro Perez, Presidente Central Bank of Costa Rica May 10, 2016 About a decade ago the Central Bank of Costa Rica (BCCR) began a process of modernization of the way in which it executes monetary policy. This process aims to ensure that Costa Rica has low and stable inflation, something that is as valid today as it was at that time. The achievement of this objective, designated in the Organic Law of the Institution, will allow Costa Ricans, especially those with greater vulnerability, to maintain their purchasing power over time. Additionally, it facilitates decision-making for entrepreneurs and other agents by having greater certainty about the expected changes in prices, in addition to reducing inequality and achieving a more efficient allocation of resources. The crisis of the early eighties triggered the application of measures that were initially expected to be temporary, but that were maintained for many years, preventing price stability for several decades. Our economy was a textbook example of a fixed exchange rate regime that made it impossible to take effective monetary policy actions to control price growth. Most Costa Ricans were certain that after a year their income would lose at least one-tenth of their purchasing power. The harmful consequences for citizens and the productive apparatus were evident, so in the middle of the last decade the BCCR made several decisions with the aim of executing its monetary policy in accordance with the mandate of its Law. First, the Bank initiated the transition to greater exchange rate flexibility and introduced changes in the way it managed liquidity with the aim of using the interest rate as an instrument of monetary control; This allows the policy rate to send realistic signals to the financial sector about the relative cost of liquidity. For this reason, the Bank implemented a new exchange rate regime that would give flexibility to the exchange rate of the US dollar, allowing it to fluctuate within limits announced to the public. In 2006 this regime was announced as temporary, with the purpose of gradually adapting the economy to increasing flexibility to facilitate the move towards a floating exchange rate regime. This decision was finally taken at the beginning of 2015. Inflation expectations and the price results of recent years show that the changes undertaken by the BCCR have made it possible for us to be close to consolidating low and stable inflation. The way monetary policy is conducted and the current exchange rate regime have allowed inflation to fall from double digits to a level similar to that of our major trading partners. The Costa Rican economy has had the privilege of making these decisions in contexts of relative economic stability. Emergency circumstances have forced many countries to adopt exchange rate easing as a last resort, after experiencing severe adjustments in real and financial variables, which tends to be costly in terms of efficiency and equity. None of the countries that migrated towards greater exchange rate easing have experienced regime-related problems when faced with economic crisis scenarios; Nor have they reversed the decision to give greater participation to market forces in the determination of the exchange rate. Even more relevant is to note that, even in adverse economic circumstances, none of these countries has abandoned floating regimes or has considered doing so in the future. Economic variables confirm what was expected when such measures were taken. The main effects of the 2008 international financial crisis on the national economy were managed by the BCCR without major costs thanks to the changes made. Foreign exchange earnings due to an increase in external indebtedness, both from the Government and the private sector, pushed the nominal exchange rate down, as expected by the forces of supply and demand. In response, the BCCR has actively participated in accumulating dollars for reserve strengthening programs and managing purchases by the non-bank public sector, which on the one hand allow resources to be available when this flow is reversed, especially if the reversal is sudden, and on the other hand attenuate the effect on the external sector of the national economy. This has allowed the Costa Rican foreign exchange market to remain stable despite the fact that external financial markets experience high volatility. This stability has been beneficial in maintaining domestic prices of imported products without considerable variations, benefiting the final consumer, and will eventually lead to greater confidence in the current exchange rate regime. In the short term, the external sector is relatively stable, so a significant adjustment in the exchange rate is not anticipated. Capital flows and foreign direct investment have been consistent with the current account deficit of the balance of payments, suggesting that the level of the exchange rate is consistent with the current state of the economy's fundamentals. Core inflation indicators indicate that medium-term price growth remains in positive territory. Inflation, as measured by the Consumer Price Index, is temporarily negative, primarily because of international price shocks and the global economic slowdown, particularly China's. However, given the current price level, it is expected that these factors will stop pushing prices down. The Central Bank has made monetary policy decisions consistent with the above, as well as with the level of production and the inflation target. It therefore reduced the policy rate by 3.5 percentage points from January 2015 to date, which is currently at the lowest level in its history. This has the potential to improve economic performance by reducing unnecessary costs for the possession of colones to the agents of the economy. Inflation is expected to return to values close to target over the medium term. The national economy has experienced an acceleration in economic activity since the fourth quarter of 2015, sustained for several months and expected to continue in the medium term. This growth in economic activity does not come exclusively from a single activity, but is a general phenomenon of the economy, which is a positive sign about sustainability and the ability to improve the well-being of the majority of the population. Our economic activity results contrast with those observed in Latin America and other emerging countries. We are one of the fastest growing countries with lower inflations, a result that may be counterintuitive to some people, but demonstrates the empirically verifiable advantages of maintaining price stability. The economic recovery motivates discussion of the problem of unemployment in our country, which has remained relatively high in recent years. It seems that there are structural factors that have prevented employment growth despite the economic upturn, a situation that constitutes a challenge in the medium term for public policies. There is no match between the needs of employers and the characteristics of those seeking employment, since production and exports increasingly require people with higher technical qualifications, while the supply of such workers cannot be expanded in the short term. However, the economic recovery we are currently experiencing has the potential to further increase employer confidence so that payrolls are increased and thereby contribute to reducing unemployment. There are other variables that affect the results of the national economy that although we would like a central bank to be able to control directly, it cannot do so. The element of greatest risk and importance and that also has consequences on the external balance of the economy is the fiscal deficit. Fortunately, low inflation and prudent management of financing needs have allowed, so far, that this shortfall in the government's budget has been financed in the domestic market without an increase in interest rates, which has given room to generate an economic recovery. This in turn has the potential to moderately increase government revenues. However, reforms must be approved and measures taken to divert the deficit from the unsustainable trajectory it has maintained over the past five years. The last aspect worth mentioning is the issue of competitiveness. The competitiveness of Costa Rican companies has always been based on the quality of the workforce and the capacity for innovation and adaptability to the changing environment of the international economy. Costa Rica has remained an attractive place to invest, thanks in part to economic and social stability, as well as its positioning within the global production chain. We must not make the mistake of thinking that an induced movement of the exchange rate, which does not respond to market forces, will make us competitive. It is possible that some activities linked to the international market will instantly become even more profitable, but that condition would quickly be lost when passed on to domestic costs. It is right that other countries have experienced depreciations of their currencies, which are due to the fact that they are exporters of raw materials whose price has fallen, which has affected not only their terms of trade but economic activity in general. However, these countries are rather actively fighting against currency depreciation to avoid further problems, as these movements have considerably eroded the purchasing power of their inhabitants, so they have had to take measures to contain inflationary pressures. This inevitably slows down those economies. In Costa Rica we have the opposite effect, and we have been able to face it successfully thanks to the flexibility of our exchange market. Fortunately, even under current conditions, there is still room for local productivity gains to remain competitive and encourage consumption of our goods and services in international markets. It is up to all Costa Ricans to achieve this.
text_original: E:\Trabajos\Identidad BCCR\Encabezado-comunicado-2011.jpg El Banco Central, inflacin y crecimiento econmico Por: Olivier Castro Prez, Presidente Banco Central de Costa Rica 10 de Mayo de 2016 Hace aproximadamente una dcada el Banco Central de Costa Rica (BCCR) inici un proceso de modernizacin sobre la forma en la que ejecuta la poltica monetaria. Este proceso aspira a lograr que Costa Rica tenga una inflacin baja y estable, algo que es tan vlido en la actualidad como lo era en ese momento. La consecucin de este objetivo, designado en la Ley Orgnica de la Institucin, permitir a los costarricenses, especialmente los de mayor vulnerabilidad, mantener su capacidad adquisitiva a lo largo del tiempo. Adicionalmente, facilita a los empresarios y a otros agentes la toma de decisiones al contar con mayor certidumbre sobre los cambios esperados en los precios, adems de reducir la inequidad y lograr una asignacin ms eficiente de los recursos. La crisis de inicios de los aos ochenta desencaden en la aplicacin de medidas que en un inicio se prevea fueran temporales, pero que se mantuvieron por muchos aos, impidiendo por varias dcadas que se lograra la estabilidad de precios. Nuestra economa era un ejemplo de libro de texto de un rgimen cambiario fijo que imposibilitaba acciones de poltica monetaria eficaces para el control del crecimiento de los precios. La mayora de costarricenses tena la certeza de que al transcurrir un ao su ingreso perdera, al menos, una dcima parte de su capacidad de compra. Las consecuencias perjudiciales para los ciudadanos y el aparato productivo eran evidentes, por lo que a mediados de la dcada pasada el BCCR tom varias decisiones con el objetivo de ejecutar su poltica monetaria en congruencia con el mandato de su Ley. En primera instancia, el Banco inici la transicin hacia una mayor flexibilidad cambiaria e introdujo cambios en la forma en que administraba la liquidez con el propsito de utilizar la tasa de inters como instrumento de control monetario; esto permite que por medio de la tasa de poltica monetaria se enven seales realistas al sector financiero sobre el costo relativo de la liquidez. Por esta razn, el Banco implement un nuevo rgimen cambiario que diera flexibilidad a la cotizacin del dlar estadounidense, permitiendo que fluctuara dentro de lmites anunciados al pblico. En el 2006 este rgimen se anunci como temporal, con el propsito de que gradualmente la economa se adaptara a una flexibilidad creciente para facilitar el moverse hacia un rgimen de flotacin cambiaria. Esta decisin fue tomada finalmente a inicios del 2015. Las expectativas de inflacin y los resultados de los ltimos aos en los precios demuestran que los cambios emprendidos por el BCCR han hecho posible que estemos cerca de consolidar una inflacin baja y estable. La forma de ejecutar la poltica monetaria y el rgimen cambiario actual han permitido que la inflacin se redujera de dos dgitos a un nivel similar al de nuestros principales socios comerciales. La economa costarricense ha tenido el privilegio de tomar estas decisiones en contextos de relativa estabilidad econmica. Circunstancias de emergencia han forzado a muchos pases a adoptar la flexibilizacin cambiaria como un recurso de ltima instancia, despus de experimentar ajustes severos en las variables reales y financieras, lo cual tiende a ser costoso en trminos de eficiencia y equidad. Ninguno de los pases que migraron hacia una mayor flexibilizacin en el tipo de cambio ha experimentado problemas relacionados con el rgimen cuando se enfrentan a escenarios de crisis econmica; tampoco han reversado la decisin de dar mayor participacin a las fuerzas del mercado en la determinacin del tipo de cambio. An ms relevante resulta anotar que, incluso en coyunturas econmicas adversas, ninguno de estos pases ha abandonado los regmenes de flotacin o ha considerado hacerlo en un futuro. Las variables econmicas confirman lo que se esperaba al tomar dichas medidas. Los principales efectos de la crisis financiera internacional del 2008 sobre la economa nacional fueron administrados por el BCCR sin mayores costos gracias a los cambios realizados. El ingreso de divisas debido a un incremento en el endeudamiento externo, tanto del Gobierno como del sector privado, presion el nivel del tipo de cambio nominal a la baja, como era de esperar por las fuerzas de la oferta y la demanda. Como respuesta el BCCR ha participado activamente acumulando dlares para los programas de fortalecimiento de reservas y administrando las compras del sector pblico no bancario, que por una parte permiten tener recursos cuando este flujo se revierta, especialmente si la reversin es repentina, y por otra parte atenan el efecto sobre el sector externo de la economa nacional. Esto ha permitido que el mercado cambiario costarricense tenga estabilidad a pesar de que los mercados financieros externos experimenten alta volatilidad. Esta estabilidad ha sido beneficiosa para mantener los precios internos de los productos importados sin variaciones considerables, beneficiando al consumidor final, y eventualmente conducir a una mayor confianza en el rgimen cambiario vigente. En el corto plazo el sector externo presenta una relativa estabilidad, por lo que no se anticipa un ajuste significativo del tipo de cambio. Los flujos de capitales y la inversin extranjera directa han sido coherentes con el dficit de cuenta corriente de la balanza de pagos lo cual sugiere que el nivel de tipo de cambio es congruente con el estado actual de los fundamentales de la economa. Los indicadores de inflacin subyacente sealan que el crecimiento de los precios de mediano plazo se mantiene en terreno positivo. La inflacin, medida con el ndice de precios al consumidor, es temporalmente negativa, primordialmente por los choques de precios internacionales y la desaceleracin econmica mundial, particularmente la de China. No obstante, dado el nivel de precios actual, es esperable que estos factores dejen de presionar los precios a la baja. El Banco Central ha tomado decisiones de poltica monetaria congruentes con lo comentado anteriormente, as como con el nivel de produccin y la meta de inflacin. Por ello redujo la tasa de poltica monetaria en 3,5 puntos porcentuales desde enero del 2015 hasta la fecha, la cual actualmente se encuentra en el nivel ms bajo de su historia. Esto tiene el potencial de mejorar el desempeo econmico al reducir costos innecesarios por la tenencia de colones a los agentes de la economa. Es esperable que la inflacin regrese a valores cercanos a la meta en el mediano plazo. La economa nacional ha experimentado una aceleracin en la actividad econmica desde el cuarto trimestre del 2015, sostenido durante varios meses y que se espera se mantenga en el mediano plazo. Este crecimiento en la actividad econmica no proviene exclusivamente de una sola actividad, sino que es un fenmeno general de la economa, lo cual es una seal positiva acerca de la sostenibilidad y la capacidad de mejorar el bienestar de la mayor parte de la poblacin. Nuestros resultados de actividad econmica contrastan con lo observado en Latinoamrica y otros pases emergentes. Somos uno de los pases que ms crece y que muestra inflaciones menores, un resultado que puede resultar contraintuitivo para algunas personas, pero que demuestra las ventajas verificables empricamente de mantener la estabilidad de precios. La recuperacin econmica motiva discutir el problema del desempleo en nuestro pas, el cual se ha mantenido relativamente alto en los ltimos aos. Al parecer hay factores estructurales que han impedido aumentar el empleo a pesar del repunte econmico, situacin que constituye un reto en el mediano plazo para las polticas pblicas. No existe un aparejamiento entre las necesidades de los empleadores con las caractersticas de aquellos que buscan empleo, ya que la produccin y las exportaciones requieren cada vez personas con mayores calificaciones tcnicas, mientras que la oferta de este tipo de trabajadores no se puede expandir en el corto plazo. No obstante, la recuperacin econmica que experimentamos en la actualidad tiene el potencial de incrementar an ms la confianza de los empleadores de manera que se incrementen las planillas y con ello contribuir a reducir el nivel de desempleo. Hay otras variables que afectan los resultados de la economa nacional que aunque quisiramos que un banco central pudiera controlar de manera directa, no lo puede hacer. El elemento de mayor riesgo e importancia y que tambin tiene consecuencias sobre el equilibrio externo de la economa es el dficit fiscal. Afortunadamente, la baja inflacin y la administracin prudente de las necesidades de financiamiento han permitido, hasta el momento que este faltante en el presupuesto del Gobierno haya podido ser financiado en el mercado interno sin un incremento de tasas de inters, lo cual ha dado espacio para generar una recuperacin econmica. Esto a la vez tiene el potencial de incrementar moderadamente los ingresos del Gobierno. No obstante, se deben aprobar las reformas y tomar medidas para desviar el dficit de la trayectoria insostenible que ha mantenido en el ltimo quinquenio. El ltimo aspecto que vale la pena mencionar es el tema de la competitividad. La competitividad de las empresas costarricenses siempre se ha basado en la calidad de la mano de obra y la capacidad de innovacin y adaptabilidad al entorno cambiante de la economa internacional. Costa Rica se ha mantenido como un lugar atractivo para invertir, en parte gracias a la estabilidad econmica y social, as como por su posicionamiento dentro de la cadena productiva mundial. No debemos cometer el error de pensar que un movimiento inducido del tipo de cambio, que no responda a las fuerzas del mercado, va a hacernos competitivos. Es posible que de manera instantnea algunas actividades vinculadas al mercado internacional se vuelvan an ms rentables, pero esa condicin rpidamente se perdera al transmitirse a los costos internos. Es correcto que otros pases han experimentado depreciaciones de sus monedas, que se deben a que son exportadores de materias primas cuyo precio ha cado, lo cual ha afectado no solo sus trminos de intercambio sino la actividad econmica en general. Sin embargo, estos pases ms bien luchan activamente en contra de la depreciacin de la moneda para evitar mayores problemas, ya que estos movimientos han erosionado considerablemente la capacidad adquisitiva de sus habitantes, por lo que han tenido que adoptar medidas para contener las presiones inflacionarias. Esto, inevitablemente, desacelera esas economas. En Costa Rica tenemos el efecto contrario, y lo hemos podido enfrentar exitosamente gracias a la flexibilidad de nuestro mercado cambiario. Afortunadamente, incluso en las condiciones actuales, existe todava espacio para aumentos de la productividad local que permitan mantener la competitividad y fomentar el consumo de nuestros bienes y servicios en los mercados internacionales. Nos corresponde a todos los costarricenses lograrlo.

Title: Competitiveness, exchange rate, employment and inflation
text: Competitiveness, exchange rate, employment and inflation By: Olivier Castro Perez, Presidente Central Bank of Costa Rica June 1, 2016 Various groups and professionals who contribute to forming opinions in the financial and economic field insist that greater economic growth and lower unemployment could be achieved if the Central Bank of Costa Rica (BCCR) modified its monetary and exchange rate policies. I would like to dedicate a few lines to explain the position of the Central Bank on these issues. Competitiveness What are we talking about? Competitiveness is the ability of an economic agent to produce a good at a lower cost or with a higher quality than its competitor. To argue that an increase in the nominal exchange rate increases national productivity and makes our goods and services cheaper in foreign markets is to ignore the interaction of these economic variables with the rest of the economy. The economic literature and empirical evidence are clear in indicating that to improve competitiveness in a sustained manner, what is required is to increase productivity. Productivity is fundamentally determined by the quality and quantity of the factors of production, the use of appropriate technologies, infrastructure and the quality of public policies, including macroeconomic stability, the latter being the main task entrusted by society to the BCCR. In support of this idea, the World Economic Forum has stressed that to increase productivity countries must improve health, education, market efficiency (products and labor), promote the efficiency of the financial system, support innovation and, to the extent possible, expand the markets in which they participate. As can be seen, monetary and exchange rate policies where they can have an effect is with regard to the financial system, the improvements in the rest of the areas correspond to other instances both public and private. So how does the BCCR contribute to improving productivity? With its macroeconomic policy and in accordance with the mandate of law, the Central Bank provides internal and external stability of the currency. Low and stable inflation facilitates economic calculation for saving and investment decisions, with effects on economic growth and employment. Lower inflation also promotes the stability of other macro prices (interest rates, exchange rates, and wages), reduces the erosion of purchasing power (particularly for fixed and low-income groups), and creates an appropriate environment for other policy areas to generate outcomes compatible with greater population welfare. The BCCR also promotes the stability and competitiveness of the financial system. It remains to mention that it acts as a lender of last resort in periods of financial stress as well as trying to maintain an adequate level of international reserves that serves as a financial shield against external shocks. Exchange rate The nominal exchange rate is a price that balances the quantities demanded and supplied of dollars in the market, so its level is certainly not determined by the BCCR. The current level of the exchange rate is the result of the objective conditions of the economy. It is true that there are distorting elements of this reality such as the high fiscal deficit and the favorable shock in the terms of trade but, again, this is not the product of inadequate policies of the Central Bank. Some specialists point out that the country has lost competitiveness and justify their claim in a calculation of what is called the real exchange rate. Based on purchasing power parity theory, it is argued that if the real factors that determine competitiveness remained fixed over time, one way to maintain invariable competitiveness would be to modify the nominal exchange rate by the equivalent of the difference between domestic inflation and international inflation. Using this methodology for Costa Rica could mislead to the conclusion that an increase in the nominal exchange rate is required to bring the real exchange rate closer to an assumed equilibrium, where other economic conditions prevailed. However, the economic literature is emphatic in indicating that this methodology is not adequate to infer deviations from the equilibrium of the real exchange rate. In contrast, the BCCR uses estimates of the equilibrium real exchange rate based on reduced structural models and statistical filters that are then combined into a single measurement to have a more robust indicator of equilibrium. The results obtained reflect that the real effective exchange rate observed is consistent with its macroeconomic determinants. For this reason, from the point of view of monetary and exchange rate policies, it is neither necessary nor prudent to make any adjustment artificially. Using the nominal exchange rate to induce changes in the real exchange rate is ineffective. One explanation for this is that there is a pass-through effect that causes the depreciation of the colon to increase the domestic prices of goods and services linked to the international market, generating inertia in price growth. After a few months this would end up offsetting the initial effect on the real exchange rate. Moreover, if economic agents anticipate that the Central Bank continuously causes depreciations in order to artificially increase competitiveness, the pass-through effect would be greater and faster. For this reason, it is inevitable to conclude that exchange rate interventions tend to be ineffective and costly, as international experience suggests. The only effective way to modify the real exchange rate is to act on the factors that determine it, those that directly affect the country's productivity. Employment and inflation An additional concern that frequently manifests itself in public discussion is the impact of the BCCR's monetary policy on employment. With regard to this issue, it is clear to the BCCR that there can be no sustained and inclusive economic growth with high unemployment. However, the determinants of employment are mostly related to factors such as internal and external business cycles, a nation's human capital, and the structure of the labor market. None of these factors can be directly affected by the policy of a central bank. The idea of a relationship between inflation and unemployment is not new, it has its origin in the economic concept developed by A.W. Phillips (1958) which is known as the Phillips curve. According to this approach, real wages would fall in the face of increases in inflation, which incentivizes employers to hire more labor. While this may be logical in a static analysis of the economy, it is not consistent with dynamic behavior. In practice, what happens is that high inflations cause workers to demand increases in the following wage negotiations to compensate for their loss of purchasing power. If high levels of inflation persist, wages tend to be indexed to past inflation, which will generate higher production costs in the future and in the end employers will have no incentive to hire more staff. An inflationary process triggered by the desire to reduce unemployment can destroy the macroeconomic stability of a country, causing greater uncertainty about economic activity among employers, so they would be more cautious in their investment and hiring decisions, increasing unemployment and probably lowering their level of production. Changes in the global economy have led in a few decades to transformations in the country's productive structure, generating an imbalance between the skills sought by employers and those offered by unemployed people. This structural unemployment, as it has been called, is not a consequence of the policies of the Central Bank. An employment policy must be aimed at facilitating the unemployed rapid insertion into the mass of employed, which considers training according to the needs of employment within the economy. Employment is and will undoubtedly be a concern of policymakers, and it is clear that the solution to the high level of unemployment in the economy is not simple. However, it is crucial to understand that higher inflation or an increase in the exchange rate will not solve the problem. Conversely, these choices may be more detrimental by widening the gap between labour demand and supply in the tradable sector, while reducing hiring capacity in the non-tradable sector of the economy. The Central Bank must be the guarantor of the country's macroeconomic stability To achieve this, it must contribute to an adequate environment for investment and job creation and ensure that inflation does not distort such decisions or deteriorate the incomes of Costa Ricans. The BCCR has maintained a monetary policy consistent with the international environment, with its objectives and with the risks present in the economy. Since the last quarter of 2014, it has adopted an expansionary monetary policy in line with projected inflation, the permanence of inflation expectations within the target range, the slack in production capacity and the existence of low external inflationary pressures. This policy supports efforts to promote a higher level of economic activity and thereby contributes to the reduction of unemployment.
text_original: E:\Trabajos\Identidad BCCR\Encabezado-comunicado-2011.jpg Competitividad, tipo de cambio, empleo e inflacin Por: Olivier Castro Prez, Presidente Banco Central de Costa Rica 1 de Junio de 2016 Diversos grupos y profesionales que contribuyen a formar opinin en el campo financiero y econmico insisten en que se podra lograr un mayor crecimiento econmico y un menor desempleo si el Banco Central de Costa Rica (BCCR) modificara sus polticas monetaria y cambiaria. Quiero dedicar unas lneas para exponer la posicin del Banco Central en estos temas. Competitividad De qu estamos hablando? La competitividad es la capacidad de un agente econmico para producir un bien a un menor costo o con una calidad mayor que su competidor. Argumentar que mediante un aumento en el tipo de cambio nominal se incrementa la productividad nacional y se abaratan nuestros bienes y servicios en los mercados externos implica ignorar la interaccin de estas variables econmicas con el resto de la economa. La literatura econmica y la evidencia emprica son claras en indicar que para mejorar la competitividad de forma sostenida, lo que se requiere es aumentar la productividad. La productividad est determinada fundamentalmente por la calidad y cantidad de los factores de la produccin, el uso de tecnologas apropiadas, la infraestructura y la calidad de las polticas pblicas, entre ellas la estabilidad macroeconmica, siendo esta ltima la principal tarea encomendada por la sociedad al BCCR. En apoyo a esta idea, el Foro Econmico Mundial ha destacado que para aumentar la productividad los pases han de mejorar la salud, la educacin, la eficiencia de los mercados (productos y laboral), promover la eficiencia del sistema financiero, apoyar la innovacin y en la medida de lo posible expandir los mercados en los que se participa. Como se puede observar, las polticas monetaria y cambiaria en donde pueden tener efecto es en lo que respecta al sistema financiero, las mejoras en el resto de mbitos corresponde a otras instancias tanto pblicas como privadas. Entonces, cmo contribuye el BCCR a mejorar la productividad? Con su poltica macroeconmica y en congruencia con el mandato de ley, el Banco Central provee estabilidad interna y externa de la moneda. Una inflacin baja y estable facilita el clculo econmico para la toma de decisiones de ahorro e inversin, con efectos sobre el crecimiento econmico y el empleo. Una menor inflacin tambin promueve la estabilidad de otros macroprecios (tasas de inters, tipo de cambio y salarios), reduce la erosin del poder de compra (particularmente para los grupos de ingresos fijos y bajos), y crea un entorno apropiado para que otras reas de la poltica generen resultados compatibles con un mayor bienestar de la poblacin. El BCCR tambin promueve la estabilidad y competitividad del sistema financiero. Resta mencionar que acta como prestamista de ltima instancia en perodos de tensin financiera al igual que procura mantener un nivel adecuado de reservas internacionales que sirva como blindaje financiero ante choques externos. Tipo de cambio El tipo de cambio nominal es un precio que equilibra las cantidades demandadas y ofrecidas de dlares en el mercado, por lo que su nivel ciertamente no est determinado por el BCCR. El nivel actual del tipo de cambio es el resultado de las condiciones objetivas de la economa. Es cierto que existen elementos distorsionantes de esta realidad como es el elevado dficit fiscal y el choque favorable en los trminos de intercambio pero, de nuevo, ello no es producto de polticas inadecuadas del Banco Central. Algunos especialistas sealan que el pas ha perdido competitividad y justifican su afirmacin en un clculo de lo que se denomina tipo de cambio real. Con base en la teora de la paridad del poder de compra, se afirma que si los factores reales que determinan la competitividad se mantuvieran fijos en el tiempo, una forma de mantener la competitividad invariable sera modificar el tipo de cambio nominal por el equivalente de la diferencia entre la inflacin interna y la inflacin internacional. Utilizar esta metodologa para Costa Rica podra inducir al error de concluir que se requiere aumentar el tipo de cambio nominal para hacer que el tipo de cambio real se aproxime a un supuesto equilibrio, donde prevalecan otras condiciones econmicas. No obstante, la literatura econmica es enftica en indicar que esta metodologa no es adecuada para inferir desviaciones respecto del equilibrio del tipo de cambio real. En contraste, el BCCR utiliza estimaciones del tipo de cambio real de equilibrio que parten de modelos estructurales reducidos y de filtros estadsticos que posteriormente se combinan en una sola medicin para tener un indicador ms robusto del equilibrio. Los resultados obtenidos reflejan que el tipo de cambio efectivo real observado es coherente con sus determinantes macroeconmicos. Por esta razn, desde el punto de vista de las polticas monetaria y cambiaria no se considera necesario ni prudente realizar artificialmente ajuste alguno. El utilizar el tipo de cambio nominal para inducir cambios en el tipo de cambio real carece de efectividad. Una explicacin para esto es que existe un efecto traspaso que ocasiona que la depreciacin del coln incremente los precios domsticos de los bienes y servicios vinculados al mercado internacional, generando inercia en el crecimiento de los precios. Al cabo de unos meses esto terminara compensando el efecto inicial sobre el tipo de cambio real. Es ms, si los agentes econmicos anticipan que el Banco Central continuamente provoca depreciaciones con el fin de incrementar artificialmente la competitividad, el efecto traspaso sera mayor y ms rpido. Por esta razn es inevitable concluir que las intervenciones cambiarias tienden a ser inefectivas y costosas, tal y como lo sugiere la experiencia internacional. La nica manera efectiva de modificar el tipo de cambio real es actuar sobre los factores que lo determinan, aquellos que inciden directamente en la productividad del pas. Empleo e inflacin Una inquietud adicional que se manifiesta con frecuencia en la discusin pblica es el impacto de la poltica monetaria del BCCR sobre el empleo. Con respecto a este tema, es claro para el BCCR que no puede existir un crecimiento econmico sostenido e inclusivo con alto desempleo. Sin embargo, los determinantes del empleo estn mayoritariamente relacionados con factores como los ciclos econmicos internos y externos, el capital humano de una nacin, y la estructura del mercado laboral. Ninguno de estos factores puede ser afectado directamente por la poltica de un banco central. La idea de una relacin entre la inflacin y el desempleo no es nueva, tiene su origen en el concepto econmico desarrollado por A.W. Phillips (1958) que se conoce como curva de Phillips. De acuerdo con este planteamiento, los salarios reales caeran ante aumentos en la inflacin, lo cual incentiva a los empresarios a contratar ms mano de obra. Si bien ello puede resultar lgico en un anlisis esttico de la economa, no es congruente con el comportamiento dinmico. En la prctica, lo que ocurre es que inflaciones altas hacen que en las siguientes negociaciones salariales los trabajadores exijan incrementos para compensar su prdida de poder adquisitivo. Si persisten niveles altos de inflacin, los salarios tienden a indexarse a la inflacin pasada, lo cual generar mayores costos de produccin en el futuro y al final de cuentas los empresarios no tendrn incentivos para contratar ms personal. Un proceso inflacionario desencadenado por el deseo de reducir el desempleo puede acabar con la estabilidad macroeconmica de un pas, provocando mayor incertidumbre sobre la actividad econmica entre los empleadores, por lo que seran ms cautos en sus decisiones de inversin y contratacin de personal, aumentando el desempleo y probablemente bajando su nivel de produccin. Los cambios en la economa global han conducido en pocas dcadas a transformaciones en la estructura productiva del pas, generando un desbalance entre las habilidades que buscan los empleadores y las que ofrecen las personas desempleadas. Este desempleo estructural, como se le ha llamado, no es consecuencia de las polticas del Banco Central. Una poltica de empleo debe ser dirigida a facilitar al desempleado una rpida insercin en la masa de ocupados, que considere una capacitacin acorde con las necesidades de empleo dentro de la economa. Indiscutiblemente el empleo es y ser una preocupacin de las autoridades encargadas de poltica econmica, y es claro que la solucin para el alto nivel de desempleo de la economa no es sencilla. No obstante, es crucial comprender que mayor inflacin o un aumento en el tipo de cambio no resolvern el problema. Por el contrario, es posible que estas opciones sean ms perjudiciales al aumentar la brecha entre la demanda de empleo y la oferta en el sector transable, mientras que reduzca la capacidad de contratacin en el sector no transable de la economa. El Banco Central debe ser el garante de la estabilidad macroeconmica del pas Para lograrlo debe contribuir a un entorno adecuado para la inversin y generacin de empleos y procurar que la inflacin no distorsione dichas decisiones ni deteriore los ingresos de los costarricenses. El BCCR ha mantenido una poltica monetaria congruente con el entorno internacional, con sus objetivos y con los riesgos presentes en la economa. Desde el ltimo trimestre del 2014 adopt una poltica monetaria expansiva en concordancia con la inflacin proyectada, la permanencia de las expectativas de inflacin dentro del rango meta, la holgura en la capacidad de produccin y la existencia de bajas presiones inflacionarias externas. Esta poltica apoya los esfuerzos por promover un mayor nivel de actividad econmica y con ello contribuye a la reduccin del desempleo.

Title: The BCCR and the foreign exchange market
text: The BCCR and the foreign exchange market San Jose, June 20, 2016 Eduardo Prado Zuniga Manager, Central Bank of Costa Rica In recent years, the Central Bank of Costa Rica (BCCR) has made decisive progress towards achieving the objectives designated by its Organic Law. Curiously, in recent weeks the media pages have published articles with names, speculations and accusations that are not consistent with an adequate historical and conjunctural analysis of the actions that the Institution has executed, especially regarding the behavior of the national exchange market. First, we must recognize that since the adoption of parity with the US dollar in 19221, Costa Rica has been characterized by fixed exchange rate regimes. Exchange rate reform, like almost any structural reform in our country, has been implemented as a slow and gradual process. It began more than three decades ago when an adjustable parity regime was adopted, which at the time managed to stabilize the economy and on that occasion the economic authorities said that it would be transitory. This transience lasted almost a quarter of a century and it was in October 2006 when a major modification was made by adopting an exchange rate band regime as a transition mechanism towards greater flexibility. It is in February 2015, when the BCCR finally formally migrates towards a more flexible regime, which it called managed floating, where the trend of the exchange rate would basically be determined by the supply and demand of foreign currency, but the bank would intervene with the purpose of moderating the volatility of this macro price; In addition, he indicated that, unlike the exchange rate band, there is no commitment regarding the level of the exchange rate. The managed float exchange rate regime is fairly new in historical terms, barely 17 months old. The changes of these policies are usually perceived with suspicion by the population, which is natural, therefore the decision of the BCCR has been balanced, allowing a growing variability of the exchange rate in the market. This is intended to ensure that economic agents progressively incorporate exchange rate risk into their decisions. This is particularly relevant for the stability of the financial system when we take into account the high level of financial dollarization. In the BCCR, we believe that greater volatility at the beginning of the new regime would have been counterproductive to its consolidation and that what was done was consistent with providing confidence in the exchange rate system and in the policy of the Central Bank in general. It is understandable that some agents consider that volatility should be higher and others think that it should be lower, but what is not correct is to affirm that the BCCR favors the stability of the exchange rate at any cost. Empirical evidence does not support that claim. In these 17 months, the minimum value of the exchange rate was 531.81 (weighted average of the Monex session of April 16, 2015) and the maximum value was 546.10 (weighted average of the Monex session of June 9, 2016), which implies a variation range of 2.7% for that period. _______________ 1 In 1922 a currency board was created in the International Bank that would be responsible for issuing notes in colones against US dollars; the exchange rate that was defined at the time was 4.0 per dollar. See, Delgado, F. (2000). Monetary policy in Costa Rica: 50 years of the Central Bank. San Jose. The Central Bank has repeatedly said that its objective, as far as it is concerned, is macroeconomic stability, not necessarily exchange rate stability. Moreover, it is clear that in order to preserve macroeconomic stability, the exchange rate must be adjusted according to the variables that determine it, it seems to us that this has been the Bank's recurring message and that its actions have been consistent with this statement. It is also necessary to mention that, unlike other regime changes, the most recent transition occurred in a context of foreign exchange inflows resulting from the Government's financing needs and shortly before a shock of considerable positive magnitude in the terms of trade. There is no doubt that these two events generated pressures on the appreciation of the national currency. In this context, the Bank explained, in great detail, that it would buy international reserves to use when the favorable terms-of-trade shock was reversed or when it faced a negative shock to external accounts, which it executed. During the last quarter of 2014 and all of 2015 the Bank accumulated reserves. Had it not done so, the exchange rate would have fallen more than was observed at the time. Conditions have now changed and the Bank has allowed the adjustment to manifest itself partly in the price (increase in the exchange rate) and partly in the reduction of the international reserves it acquired precisely for that purpose, which should not be surprising since it was announced in advance that it would proceed in this way. In short, the Bank has done exactly what it announced it would do. Interestingly, the purchase of foreign currency and moderation of the tendency to appreciate the currency was not questioned by those who today make accusations to the BCCR. Congruence would indicate that at that time they should have requested with equal vehemence a more rapid appreciation of the currency so that market forces manifested themselves more quickly. Now, they indicate that there is no congruence between the de facto and de jure regimes, so the Bank should not execute the counterparty of the actions announced in advance. It is not correct that there is a preference for exchange rate stability. The new exchange rate regime has always shown tendencies towards the appreciation and depreciation of the national currency. It is not surprising that the results of a flexible market leave some people and sectors dissatisfied; Any movement in either direction can be perceived in the short term as a benefit to one group to the detriment of another. The task of the BCCR is precisely to intervene as little as possible so that trends in the market manifest. An example of this is that in the current context in which there is an adjustment, since April 2016, with an upward trend in the exchange rate, the variation in the reserves held by the BCCR has been minimal. The variable of interest to analysts who criticize the Bank seems to be the fraction of Net International Reserves that exclude government deposits, those of financial institutions and the balance that is maintained to manage purchases of the Non-Bank Public Sector. The amount of these, instead of being reduced, has increased from December 31, 2015 to June 15, 2016 in US 44 million. We appreciate that the BCCR's action has been prudent, balanced and consistent over time. This Entity will continue to act in the foreign exchange market moderating abrupt movements, allowing the trends that dictate the long-term determinants to manifest and fully executing plans that are public knowledge that contribute to the prudent administration of the exchange market and, therefore, to macroeconomic stability in accordance with what our Law requires of us.

Curiosamente, en semanas recientes las pginas de medios de comunicacin han divulgado artculos con apelativos, especulaciones y acusaciones que no son congruentes con un anlisis histrico y coyuntural adecuado de las acciones que ha ejecutado la Institucin, especialmente referentes al comportamiento del mercado cambiario nacional. En primer trmino, debemos reconocer que desde que se adopt la paridad con el dlar de EUA, en 19221, Costa Rica se caracteriz por la vigencia de regmenes de tipo de cambio fijo. La reforma cambiaria, como casi toda reforma estructural en nuestro pas, se ha ejecutado como un proceso lento y gradual. Inici hace ms de tres dcadas cuando se adopt un rgimen de paridad ajustable, el cual en su momento logr estabilizar la economa y en esa oportunidad las autoridades econmicas dijeron que sera transitorio. Esa transitoriedad dur casi un cuarto de siglo y fue en octubre del 2006 cuando se realiz una modificacin mayscula al adoptar un rgimen de banda cambiaria como mecanismo de transicin hacia una mayor flexibilidad. Es en febrero del 2015, cuando el BCCR finalmente migra de manera formal hacia un rgimen ms flexible, que denomin flotacin administrada, donde la tendencia del tipo de cambio estara bsicamente determinada por la oferta y demanda de divisas, pero el banco intervendra con el propsito de moderar la volatilidad de este macro precio; adems, indic que, a diferencia de la banda cambiaria, no existe compromiso en cuanto al nivel del tipo de cambio. El rgimen cambiario de flotacin administrada es bastante nuevo en trminos histricos, tiene apenas 17 meses de vida. Los cambios de estas polticas usualmente son percibidos con recelo por la poblacin, lo cual es natural, por tanto la decisin del BCCR ha sido balanceada, permitiendo una variabilidad creciente del tipo de cambio en el mercado. Se pretende con ello que los agentes econmicos, progresivamente, incorporen el riesgo cambiario en sus decisiones. Esto es particularmente relevante para la estabilidad del sistema financiero cuando tomamos en cuenta el alto nivel de dolarizacin financiera. En el BCCR consideramos que una volatilidad mayor al inicio del nuevo rgimen hubiese sido contraproducente para su consolidacin y que lo actuado fue coherente con proveer confianza en el sistema cambiario y en la poltica del Banco Central en general. Es entendible que algunos agentes consideren que la volatilidad debera ser mayor y que otros opinen que debera ser menor, pero lo que no es correcto es afirmar que el BCCR privilegia la estabilidad del tipo de cambio a cualquier costo. La evidencia emprica no apoya esa afirmacin. En estos 17 meses, el valor mnimo del tipo de cambio fue 531,81 (promedio ponderado de la sesin de Monex del 16 de abril del 2015) y el valor mximo fue 546,10 (promedio ponderado de la sesin de Monex del 9 de junio del 2016), lo que implica un rango de variacin de 2,7% para ese perodo. _______________ 1 En 1922 se crea una caja de conversin en el Banco Internacional que sera la encargada de emitir billetes en colones contra dlares de EUA; el tipo de cambio que se defini en su momento fue de 4,0 por dlar. Ver, Delgado, F. (2000). La poltica monetaria en Costa Rica: 50 aos del Banco Central. San Jos. El Banco Central reiteradamente ha dicho que su objetivo, en lo que le corresponde, es la estabilidad macroeconmica, no necesariamente la estabilidad cambiaria. Es ms, es claro que para preservar la estabilidad macroeconmica se requiere que el tipo de cambio se ajuste de acuerdo con las variables que lo determinan, nos parece que este ha sido el mensaje recurrente del Banco y que su actuacin ha sido coherente con dicho enunciado. Es necesario tambin mencionar que, a diferencia de otros cambios de rgimen, la transicin ms reciente ocurri en un contexto de ingreso de divisas producto de las necesidades de financiamiento del Gobierno y con poca antelacin a un choque de magnitud positiva considerable en los trminos de intercambio. No hay duda de que estos dos eventos generaron presiones a la apreciacin de la moneda nacional. En ese contexto, el Banco explic, con sumo detalle, que comprara reservas internacionales para utilizarlas en el momento que el choque favorable de los trminos de intercambio se revirtiera o cuando se enfrentara un choque negativo sobre las cuentas externas, lo cual ejecut. Durante el ltimo trimestre del 2014 y todo el 2015 el Banco acumul reservas. De no haberlo hecho, el tipo de cambio hubiese cado ms de lo que se observ en ese tiempo. En la actualidad las condiciones han cambiado y el Banco ha permitido que el ajuste se manifieste parte en el precio (aumento en el tipo de cambio) y parte en la reduccin de las reservas internacionales que adquiri precisamente para ese fin, lo cual tampoco debera ser sorpresa pues se anunci de manera anticipada que se procedera de esa forma. En resumen, el Banco ha hecho exactamente lo que anunci que hara. Curiosamente, la compra de divisas y moderacin de la tendencia a la apreciacin de la moneda no fue cuestionada por quienes hoy realizan acusaciones al BCCR. La congruencia indicara que en aquel momento debieron haber solicitado con igual vehemencia una apreciacin ms acelerada de la moneda para que se manifestaran ms rpidamente las fuerzas del mercado. Ahora, indican que no hay congruencia entre el rgimen de facto y el de iure, por lo que el Banco no debiera ejecutar la contraparte de las acciones anunciadas con antelacin. No es correcto que existe una preferencia por la estabilidad del tipo de cambio. En el nuevo rgimen cambiario siempre se han manifestado las tendencias a la apreciacin y depreciacin de la moneda nacional. No es extrao que los resultados de un mercado flexible dejen insatisfechos a algunas personas y sectores; cualquier movimiento en alguna de las dos direcciones puede percibirse en el corto plazo como un beneficio para un grupo en detrimento de otro. La labor del BCCR es precisamente intervenir lo menos posible para que se manifiesten las tendencias en el mercado. Una muestra de ello es que en el contexto actual en el que hay un ajuste, a partir de abril del 2016, con una tendencia al alza en el tipo de cambio, la variacin en las reservas en poder del BCCR ha sido mnima.
